subtopic: What a stage manager actually does
question: In your own words, what does a stage manager actually do?
lookingFor: A realistic, specific picture of the job beyond 'organising the show' — shows they've watched or worked with one, not just guessed.

bullets: Cover the full arc: rehearsal room support, running the paperwork, then running the live show
Mention specific outputs like the prompt book and calling cues
Show understanding that the SM is the communication hub between departments
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A stage manager is really the person who holds the whole production together from the first rehearsal to closing night. In the room they take blocking notes, time scenes, and make sure everyone knows the schedule, and once the show moves into the theatre they build the prompt book and actually call every cue live during the performance. What I find most interesting is that they're the hub everyone else reports through, from lighting to wardrobe to the director, so the job is as much about communication as it is about paperwork.

commonMistakes: Reducing the role to 'making sure the actors know their lines'
Describing only the rehearsal-room part and ignoring the live-calling side
Confusing stage manager with director
followUps: Which part of that job do you think you'd find hardest?

subtopic: Why stage management over directing or acting
question: You clearly love theatre. Why stage management rather than directing or acting?
lookingFor: Genuine self-knowledge about what draws them to a supporting, structural role rather than a performing or creative-lead one.

bullets: Reflect honestly on temperament and where they find satisfaction
Contrast the SM role with directing/acting without putting those roles down
Back it with a real experience where they preferred running things to being in the spotlight
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I acted in a couple of school plays and enjoyed it, but I noticed I was far more excited backstage watching the whole machine work than I was waiting in the wings for my cue. When I stage managed our sixth form musical, I loved that I got to see every department at once and make the thing actually happen on time. I don't need to be the person with the idea or the person on stage, I want to be the person who makes sure the idea gets to the audience exactly as intended.

commonMistakes: Implying stage management is a fallback because they weren't good enough to act or direct
Giving no concrete experience to support the preference
Sounding unsure whether they actually want this over performing
followUps: Was there a specific moment that confirmed this was the right path for you?

question: Why do you want to study stage management on this course rather than just learning on the job?
lookingFor: Specific knowledge of what the course offers and why structured training matters for this craft, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific feature of the course, like in-house productions, industry placements, or technical facilities
Explain why formal training adds something on-the-job experience can't
Connect it to their own gaps or goals
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've picked up a lot backstage already, but I've had to guess at things like proper prompt book notation or how to run a technical rehearsal, and I don't want to keep learning that by accident. Your course puts students on real in-house productions from year one and has a dedicated stage management pathway rather than folding it into general production arts, which is rare. I want the structured grounding in paperwork, health and safety, and calling technique before I'm relied on in a professional room.

commonMistakes: Answering with generic praise that would apply to any drama school
Suggesting the course is just a formality before getting a 'real' job
Not naming anything specific about the course structure
followUps: What would you want to get out of your first in-house production here?

question: What first drew you to working backstage rather than being on stage?
lookingFor: A specific, believable origin story that shows early and sustained interest rather than a rehearsed line.

bullets: Name a specific moment or production, not a vague love of theatre
Explain what about that moment appealed to them specifically
Show the interest has continued and grown since
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I was cast in a small role in our school's production of Our Town, but I ended up spending most of my free time in the wings watching the stage manager run the show with a headset and a torch, and I was completely hooked. There was something about the calm control of it, calling 'lighting cue 12, go' in the middle of chaos, that felt more thrilling to me than being on stage myself. I asked to shadow her for the next show, and I've been chasing that same feeling in every production since.

commonMistakes: Vague statements like 'I've always loved theatre' with no specific moment
Describing an interest that only started very recently with no follow-through
Making it sound like a backup plan rather than a genuine pull
followUps: Have you shadowed or assisted a professional stage manager since?

question: Talk us through a production you've worked on backstage. What was your role?
lookingFor: A concrete, specific account of real hands-on experience with clear ownership of tasks and honest scale.

bullets: Name the production, venue or company, and their exact role
Describe one or two concrete responsibilities, not a vague summary
Reflect on something they learned or would do differently
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I was assistant stage manager on our youth theatre's production of Blood Brothers last spring, working under a stage manager who'd worked professionally, which was brilliant training. My main job was running props, so I built and maintained the prop table and did the pre-show check every night, plus I took over calling one performance when our SM was ill. That night taught me how much concentration calling actually takes, I missed a cue by a beat and it made me realise how important it is to mark your script clearly in advance.

commonMistakes: Overstating a minor role as if they ran the whole show
Giving a vague summary with no specific tasks
Talking only about the production's story rather than their actual job
followUps: What would you do differently if you did that role again?

question: What is a prompt book, and why is it so central to the stage manager's job?
lookingFor: Accurate technical understanding of the prompt book as the master reference document, plus why it matters practically.

bullets: Define it as the master copy of the script with blocking, cues, and notes
Explain it's built up during rehearsals and used to run the show
Note it lets anyone take over the show if the SM is unavailable
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The prompt book is the master version of the script that the stage manager builds throughout rehearsals, with blocking, every lighting and sound cue, and any technical notes marked in against the exact line or moment they happen. It's what the SM actually calls the show from once it's in the theatre. What makes it so important is that it's not just for one person's memory, if the deputy SM or a replacement had to step in, the prompt book should let them run the show accurately from day one.

commonMistakes: Confusing it with the script itself, with no mention of blocking or cues
Not mentioning that it's built progressively through the rehearsal process
Missing why it needs to be legible and usable by someone else
followUps: How would you keep a prompt book organised during a fast-moving rehearsal?

question: How would you explain the difference between a director and a stage manager to someone who's never been backstage?
lookingFor: Clear distinction between creative authorship and the running, logistical, and communication function.

bullets: State the director shapes the artistic vision and interpretation
State the stage manager makes that vision run smoothly and safely, in rehearsal and performance
Note the SM's authority takes over once the show opens and the director steps back
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The director is the one deciding what the production means and how it should look and feel, they're making the artistic choices with the actors and designers. The stage manager is the one making sure all of that actually happens on schedule, safely, and the same way every night, they run the rehearsal room, coordinate every department, and once the show opens they're the one calling the cues and effectively in charge of the performance itself. So the director shapes it, and the stage manager delivers it consistently once it's built.

commonMistakes: Describing the stage manager as an assistant to the director with no independent authority
Missing that the SM's role changes once the show opens
Being vague enough that the two roles sound interchangeable
followUps: Whose call is it if there's a disagreement once the show has opened?

question: Can you explain the difference between the stage manager, deputy stage manager, and assistant stage manager?
lookingFor: Accurate knowledge of the standard UK stage management team hierarchy and where responsibilities split.

bullets: SM runs the overall production, schedule, and company management
DSM typically runs the book and calls the show in performance
ASM handles props, backstage running, and practical support during the show
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In most UK theatre teams, the stage manager has overall responsibility for the production, the schedule, and managing the company, while the deputy stage manager is usually the one who runs the prompt book and actually calls the cues once the show is live. The assistant stage manager, or several ASMs, handle the practical backstage running, things like props, scene changes, and quick changes during the show. It varies by company, some SMs call their own shows, but that's the structure I've learned to expect.

commonMistakes: Assuming all three titles mean the same job at different pay grades
Getting the calling responsibility backwards
Not acknowledging that structure varies between companies
followUps: Which of those three would you want to start out as, and why?

question: Give us an example of a time your organisational skills genuinely made a difference on a production.
lookingFor: A specific, credible story showing planning or systems that prevented a problem, not vague self-praise.

bullets: Describe a concrete system or process they set up, not just 'I'm organised'
Explain the problem it solved or prevented
Show they understood why it mattered to the wider production
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For our college production of Grease, I noticed our props list was scattered across three different people's notebooks, so I built a single spreadsheet with what each prop was, who was responsible for it, and which scene it appeared in. During tech week we caught a missing prop for a scene change two days before it would have been a disaster on opening night, purely because the spreadsheet flagged the gap. It taught me that organisation isn't about being tidy for its own sake, it's about building systems that catch problems before an audience ever sees them.

commonMistakes: Describing being naturally tidy with no actual example
A story where the organisation made no real difference to the outcome
Taking sole credit for what was clearly a team effort
followUps: Did that system stay in place for future productions?

question: What does it mean to 'call' a show, and what skills do you think that takes?
lookingFor: Understanding that calling means live cueing of the whole crew via headset, and the concentration and calm it demands.

bullets: Explain calling as giving live standby and go cues to lighting, sound, and other departments through the show
Note it requires reading the actors' pace, not just the clock
Mention the composure needed to keep going if something goes wrong
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Calling a show means sitting with the prompt book during the performance and giving every department their standby and go over headset, so lighting changes, sound cues, and set moves all happen at exactly the right moment. It sounds mechanical, but it isn't, because actors never deliver a line at exactly the same pace twice, so the caller has to be watching and listening in real time, not just following a stopwatch. I think it takes real concentration and a calm head, because if something goes wrong, the caller is often the only person with the overview to fix it without the audience noticing.

commonMistakes: Describing it as simply reading cues off a fixed timeline
Missing the live, responsive nature of the skill
Underselling how much pressure is involved
followUps: How do you think you'd handle calling your very first live show?

question: Why is health and safety such a central part of a stage manager's responsibility?
lookingFor: Understanding that the SM is often the person legally and practically responsible for safety backstage, with realistic examples.

bullets: Note that backstage involves real hazards, moving scenery, rigging, low light, quick changes
Explain the SM is usually the person responsible for risk assessments and safe running
Give a concrete example of a safety consideration they've encountered or can imagine
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Backstage is genuinely dangerous if it's not managed properly, you've got scenery moving in near darkness, actors doing quick changes at speed, sometimes rigging or pyrotechnics, and it's usually the stage manager who's responsible for the risk assessment and making sure everyone knows the safe way to do their job. When I ran backstage for a show with a fast set change, we taped glow tape along every trip hazard and walked the whole crew through it in slow motion before we ever tried it at speed. It made me realise safety isn't a box to tick, it's something you actually have to rehearse.

commonMistakes: Treating health and safety as paperwork rather than a practical responsibility
Giving no concrete example of a real hazard
Assuming safety is someone else's job, like the venue's
followUps: What would you do if you saw a safety issue the director wanted to ignore for the sake of the show?

question: An actor misses their entrance cue completely during a live performance. What would you do, as the person calling the show?
lookingFor: Composed, structured problem-solving that prioritises keeping the show moving and communicating clearly under pressure.

bullets: Prioritise staying calm and not freezing the rest of the cues
Describe practical options, prompting over headset, holding the next cue, or letting the other actors improvise a beat
Mention debriefing afterwards to prevent it happening again
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first job is to not panic and not let one missed cue cause a second problem, so I'd hold any dependent lighting or sound cues for a beat rather than firing them into an empty stage. If there's a way to prompt them quietly, over the wings or a headset if they're wearing one, I'd do that immediately, while trusting the other actors on stage to cover with a line or two if they're experienced enough. Once the scene is back on track I'd make a note rather than dwell on it live, and I'd want a quick, blame-free conversation afterwards about what happened and how we stop it recurring.

commonMistakes: Freezing the whole show or panicking visibly on headset
Focusing only on assigning blame rather than solving the immediate problem
No mention of a follow-up conversation to prevent repeats
followUps: How would you talk to that actor afterwards without making them feel worse?

question: What's a production you've seen recently, and what did you notice about how it was run technically?
lookingFor: Genuine, active theatre-going with a stage management eye, not just enjoyment as an audience member.

bullets: Name a specific, recent production honestly, not something they think sounds impressive
Notice something technical, a scene change, a cue, a transition, not just the story
Reflect on what that suggests about the stage management behind it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I saw a touring production of The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time last month, and what stayed with me was how seamless the scene changes were, the set is essentially a grid of lights and the transitions happened almost invisibly in the dark. It made me think about how tightly that must be called, because the lighting states and the set movement had to land within a second of each other every single time. It's the kind of show where you only really notice the stage management if it goes wrong, which is exactly why I found it so impressive.

commonMistakes: Naming a production but only discussing plot or acting
Naming something they clearly haven't actually seen
Giving no specific technical observation
followUps: Have you read any books or blogs by working stage managers?

question: What do you think goes into building a rehearsal schedule, and why is it harder than it sounds?
lookingFor: Awareness of the real constraints, actor availability, scene coverage, venue access, and the SM's role in juggling them.

bullets: Mention balancing actor and creative team availability against which scenes need to be rehearsed
Note constraints like venue access, understudies, or school and work commitments in amateur settings
Show awareness that the schedule has to flex as the production develops
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It looks simple on paper, just decide which scenes get rehearsed when, but really you're juggling which actors are needed for each scene, when they're all actually free, and how much time the director thinks each scene needs, which usually changes once rehearsals start. I helped build a schedule for a show where half the cast had day jobs, so we had to group scenes by which actors overlapped and protect certain evenings for the ones who could only come late. What made it harder than it sounds is that you have to keep adjusting it as you learn more, a scene that was meant to take an hour can suddenly need three.

commonMistakes: Treating scheduling as a purely administrative task with no real constraints
Ignoring that schedules need to be revised as rehearsals progress
No mention of the human factor, actor availability and fatigue
followUps: How would you handle a director who keeps running significantly over the scheduled time?

question: Stage management involves working closely with strong personalities, directors, designers, actors. Tell us about a time you had to manage a difficult working relationship.
lookingFor: Diplomatic, mature handling of interpersonal friction with a focus on keeping the production on track.

bullets: Describe the specific friction honestly without being unkind about the other person
Focus on the practical steps taken to keep communication working
Show the production benefited, not just that the conflict was avoided
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I worked with a designer who kept changing set requirements after they'd been agreed, which was throwing off our build schedule every time. Rather than getting frustrated in the moment, I asked to have a short weekly check-in with them specifically, so changes came through a clear channel instead of ad hoc during rehearsals. It meant I could flag the knock-on effect on the schedule immediately rather than discovering it too late, and by the end we'd actually built a good working relationship because they trusted I'd tell them honestly when something wasn't feasible.

commonMistakes: Painting the other person as simply unreasonable with no self-reflection
Describing avoidance rather than active management of the relationship
No concrete outcome or resolution
followUps: What would you do if that approach hadn't worked?

question: What happens during a technical rehearsal, and why is it usually the most stressful part of putting on a show?
lookingFor: Practical understanding of what a tech is for and why the pace and pressure are unlike ordinary rehearsals.

bullets: Explain tech is where lighting, sound, and set cues are set and integrated with the actors for the first time
Note the stop-start pace, moving cue by cue rather than running scenes
Explain the pressure comes from limited time before opening and many departments needing decisions at once
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Tech is when all the technical elements, lighting, sound, set changes, are put together with the actors for the first time, so instead of running scenes straight through you're often stopping every few minutes to set or adjust a cue. It's stressful because there's usually very little time before opening night, and every department, lighting, sound, wardrobe, needs decisions made in the room right then, often at the same time. As the stage manager you're the one keeping track of every cue that's been agreed and making sure nothing gets lost in the chaos.

commonMistakes: Confusing tech with a normal run-through rehearsal
Not explaining why the pace is stop-start rather than continuous
Missing the time-pressure element that makes it stressful
followUps: How would you keep track of changes agreed on the fly during a tech?

question: How would you go about recording an actor's blocking during a rehearsal?
lookingFor: Practical understanding of blocking notation, using the script, stage directions shorthand, and consistency across rehearsals.

bullets: Mention noting movement directly against the script line where it happens
Reference using stage direction shorthand, like DSL, USR, or similar abbreviations
Note the importance of keeping it consistent and legible for continuity
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd write the movement directly into the prompt copy against the exact line it happens on, using shorthand like DSL for downstage left or XR for cross right, so it's quick to jot down in the moment without breaking the flow of rehearsal. Consistency matters a lot, if I use my own private shorthand that no one else can read, it's useless the moment someone else needs to check continuity or a replacement has to be blocked into the show. The real skill is capturing it fast enough that you're not the reason rehearsal slows down, while still being clear enough to read back weeks later.

commonMistakes: Describing blocking as something they'd just try to remember
No mention of standard shorthand or notation conventions
Ignoring the need for it to be legible to other people later
followUps: What would you do if the blocking changed significantly between rehearsals?

question: Do you think stage managing a musical is different from stage managing a straight play? How?
lookingFor: Awareness that genre changes the practical demands of the job, not just a surface-level opinion.

bullets: Note musicals typically add music department coordination and often faster, more numerous cues
Mention costume quick-changes and choreography as added complexity in musicals
Show it isn't just 'harder', the skills required shift, e.g. working with a musical director
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think a musical adds a whole extra layer, because now you're coordinating with a musical director and a band or backing track alongside everything else, and the cueing is often much denser, with music, lighting, and choreography all needing to land together. There tend to be more quick changes too, which means backstage running has to be almost choreographed in itself. A straight play can still be technically demanding, but a musical usually asks the stage manager to coordinate more departments at a faster pace, so I'd expect the calling to be a lot busier.

commonMistakes: Saying one is simply 'easier' with no specific reasoning
Not mentioning the musical director or music department as a distinct collaborator
Overlooking quick changes and choreography as added complexity
followUps: Have you worked on a musical or a dance piece, and what surprised you about it?

question: How would you keep lighting, sound, and wardrobe all on the same page during a production?
lookingFor: Practical understanding of the SM as a communication hub, with concrete tools or habits, not just 'good communication'.

bullets: Mention concrete tools, rehearsal reports, production meetings, shared documents
Show awareness that each department needs different information at different times
Note the importance of one consistent source of truth, like the prompt book or a running order
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd rely on a daily rehearsal report, a short written summary sent out after every session flagging anything each department needs to know, a costume change added, a prop request, a set change that's shifted. On top of that I think regular production meetings matter, because some things are easier to sort out in a five-minute conversation than a written note. The key for me is having one place everyone trusts as the source of truth, so nobody's working off out-of-date information.

commonMistakes: Giving only a vague answer like 'I'd talk to everyone regularly'
Not mentioning any concrete document or system
Assuming every department needs the same information at the same time
followUps: What would you do if two departments received conflicting instructions?

subtopic: A stage management moment that impressed them
question: Tell us about a piece of stage management, in a show you've seen or read about, that genuinely impressed you.
lookingFor: Specific, informed admiration that shows the applicant looks at theatre with a technical, not just an audience, eye.

bullets: Name a specific production or documented example, not a vague generalisation
Explain precisely what impressed them technically
Show understanding of why it would have been difficult to achieve
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read an interview with the stage management team behind a West End production that ran a full scene change, furniture, lighting, and a costume change, in under fifteen seconds in total blackout, every single night for years without a single accident. What impressed me was the precision of it, that level of consistency has to come from meticulous rehearsal and a prompt book detailed enough that everyone knows their exact steps blind. It made me appreciate that the audience experiences that moment as magic, but behind it is an enormous amount of drilled, disciplined work.

commonMistakes: Praising the acting or story rather than a technical stage management detail
Being too vague to demonstrate real knowledge
Naming something they can't actually explain when pressed
followUps: What do you think it took to rehearse a change like that safely?

question: Halfway through a run, one of your lead actors is injured and can't go on tonight. As stage manager, what's your immediate response?
lookingFor: Calm, prioritised crisis management that puts safety first, then communicates clearly up and down the production.

bullets: Prioritise the actor's welfare and getting them appropriate help first
Move quickly to assess options, understudy, cover, or informing front of house
Show clear, calm communication with the company and any necessary announcements
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My very first priority is the actor themselves, making sure they're safe and getting whatever help they need, everything else waits until that's handled. Once that's underway, I'd immediately find out if there's an understudy or if someone can go on script in hand, and loop in the director and producer so a decision gets made fast, because the audience is arriving soon. I'd also make sure front of house has clear information to give the audience if there's a cast change or a delay, because keeping everyone calm and informed matters as much as solving the practical problem.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to solving the show problem before addressing the injured actor
No mention of communicating with front of house or the audience
Freezing rather than working through a clear order of priorities
followUps: What if there's no understudy and the show has to be cancelled at short notice?

question: Have you looked into how professional stage management jobs actually work, things like union agreements, contracts, or touring?
lookingFor: Some genuine research into the professional realities of the job, showing this is an informed choice rather than an idealised one.

bullets: Show some awareness that professional productions operate under union agreements, e.g. Equity in the UK
Mention practical realities like long or irregular hours, touring, or short contracts
Be honest about what they still don't know, rather than overclaiming expertise
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've read a bit about how Equity agreements set out things like minimum rest periods and how many performances a week are standard, and I know professional stage management contracts are often short and involve touring, which means the work can be unpredictable and away from home a lot. I don't pretend to know all the details yet, agreements clearly vary between companies and venues, but I wanted to go in with my eyes open rather than a romantic idea of the job. It's actually part of why I want proper training, so I understand the professional structure before I'm relying on it for a living.

commonMistakes: Claiming detailed expert knowledge of union rules with no real basis
Having done no research at all into professional working conditions
Sounding naive about the demands of touring or irregular hours
followUps: How do you feel about the touring lifestyle that a lot of professional work involves?

question: Stage managers often lead a large team but rarely get public credit. How do you feel about that?
lookingFor: Genuine comfort with a leadership role that's largely invisible to the audience, grounded in real motivation rather than false modesty.

bullets: Acknowledge honestly that public recognition matters less to them than the work itself
Explain where they do find satisfaction, for example a smooth show or a trusted team
Avoid sounding falsely self-effacing or secretly resentful
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think I'm genuinely fine with that, and I've had a small taste of it already, when a show I ran went smoothly the applause was all for the cast, and honestly that felt right to me, because the job succeeded exactly when nobody had to think about it. What I get out of it instead is quieter, watching a nervous first-time crew member run their first cue perfectly, or knowing a whole team trusted me enough to just do their jobs without worrying. I don't think I need the audience's applause, I think I need the company's trust, and that's a different kind of reward that suits me.

commonMistakes: Insisting they don't care about recognition at all in a way that sounds rehearsed
Revealing they actually resent the lack of credit
Giving no real example of where satisfaction comes from instead
followUps: Have you ever felt frustrated not getting credit for something that went well?

subtopic: Juggling multiple demands under time pressure
question: Describe a time you had to juggle several urgent tasks at once during a production. How did you decide what to do first?
lookingFor: A concrete example of prioritisation under pressure with a sensible, explainable method for ordering tasks.

bullets: Give a specific example with genuinely competing demands
Explain the reasoning behind what got done first, not just that it worked out
Show awareness of what could have gone wrong if prioritised differently
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: During get-in for our last show, I had a missing prop, a lighting rig running late, and an actor who needed a costume fitted, all inside the same twenty minutes. I decided the lighting rig had to come first because everything else in the schedule depended on it being ready before we could even start a technical run, whereas the prop and the fitting could still be squeezed in around it. I flagged both the smaller issues to the relevant people so they weren't forgotten, and dealt with them the moment the rig was sorted. It taught me that prioritising isn't about urgency alone, it's about which task everything else is waiting on.

commonMistakes: Describing a situation with no real competing pressure
No clear reasoning for the order chosen
Suggesting they just did everything at once with no actual prioritisation
followUps: What do you do when two tasks are genuinely equally urgent?

question: Where do you hope stage management takes you in the future, and how does this course fit into that?
lookingFor: A grounded, realistic sense of direction in the field, connected honestly to what the course actually offers.

bullets: Give a genuine direction of interest, for example touring theatre, opera, or company management, without over-specifying
Connect the goal honestly to what the course teaches
Show awareness that early career experience will likely shape or shift the goal
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm drawn to large-scale touring theatre, the logistics of moving a whole production between venues fascinates me as much as the show itself, though I know that might change once I've actually worked in different settings. This course appeals because it doesn't just teach calling and paperwork, it puts us through full production cycles with real technical demands, which is exactly the grounding I'd need before taking on something that complex. I'm realistic that my first jobs will probably be smaller and more varied, and I actually want that, because I'd rather build real range before narrowing down.

commonMistakes: An overly specific plan with no room for the reality of early career work
A goal disconnected from anything the course actually teaches
Sounding like stage management is a stepping stone to something else entirely
followUps: What kind of production would be your dream to stage manage one day?
